classification.difficultyReason: The student reads curved regions from the graph. Part a compares equal-width areas by height without computing them. Part b needs an extra step: split the interval and use the sign of the extra region. It is slightly more demanding than the sign and triangle arguments in p19-q4, but needs no area formulae.

content.prompt:
The diagram shows the curve $y=4-x^2$.

Without evaluating the definite integrals, explain why:

answer.short: Both regions lie above the $x$-axis and have width $1$, but the curve is higher on $[0,1]$, so that area is larger.
answer.worked:
Both intervals have width $1$ and the curve lies above the $x$-axis on $0\le x\le2$, so both integrals are areas.
The curve is decreasing, so it is higher on $[0,1]$ than on $[1,2]$. The area on $[0,1]$ is larger, so $\displaystyle\int_0^1(4-x^2)\,dx>\int_1^2(4-x^2)\,dx$.

answer.short: The extra interval $[2,3]$ lies below the $x$-axis, so it subtracts from the signed area.
answer.worked:
Split the interval at $x=2$:
$$\int_{-2}^{3}(4-x^2)\,dx=\int_{-2}^{2}(4-x^2)\,dx+\int_{2}^{3}(4-x^2)\,dx$$
On $[2,3]$ the curve lies below the $x$-axis, so $\displaystyle\int_2^3(4-x^2)\,dx<0$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3}(4-x^2)\,dx<\int_{-2}^{2}(4-x^2)\,dx$.
